analysis.one_liner: Gives internet users rights over their personal data and creates a new federal privacy agency to enforce them.
analysis.headline: The Online Privacy Act never got a committee markup or a floor vote in the 117th Congress, dying in committee with 8 Democratic supporters and no Republican ones.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give people enforceable rights over the personal data companies collect about them: the right to see it, correct it, delete it, take it to another service, and say no to targeted ads and algorithmic decisions, with a human reviewing the decision on request. It would require companies to collect less data, get clear consent before selling or sharing it, stop manipulative 'dark patterns' in consent screens, and notify users of breaches. It would create a new Digital Privacy Agency to enforce the rules, allow state attorneys general and individuals to sue, and make doxxing intended to intimidate someone a federal crime. The bill was referred to three House committees and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet gains concrete rights: to know what data a company holds and where it got it, to fix or erase it, to move it to a competitor, to opt out of behavioral profiling and targeted advertising, to get a human review of decisions made solely by algorithms, and to be told when their data is breached. Workers, renters, and borrowers also gain protection against ads for jobs, housing, credit, and insurance being targeted or withheld by race, sex, disability, or other protected traits. People targeted by doxxing gain a federal criminal remedy. Small businesses are carved out of most duties.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals would get rights to access, correct, delete, and port their personal data, including a list of which third parties a company shared it with and how it was obtained.

Companies could not use people's data for behavioral personalization or targeted profiling without affirmative express consent, renewed at least yearly, and could not charge fees for exercising privacy rights.

The bill prohibits processing personal data in ways that discriminate by race, sex, disability, and other protected classes in job, credit, insurance, housing, and education opportunities, and bans 'dark patterns' that trick people in consent processes.

It creates a Digital Privacy Agency with investigation and litigation powers, lets state attorneys general and individuals sue, protects whistleblowers, and voids predispute arbitration agreements for claims under the Act.

It requires notification of data breaches and data-sharing abuse, restricts companies' use of the contents of communications, and adds a federal crime — up to 5 years in prison — for disclosing personal information with intent to threaten, intimidate, or harass.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that make money collecting, processing, and selling personal data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large online platforms — would bear compliance costs, lose targeted-advertising data flows that require consent, and face enforcement by a new agency plus private lawsuits. Firms above the small-business thresholds (under $25 million revenue, fewer than 200 employees, data on fewer than 250,000 people, and not earning revenue from selling personal information) would have to meet data-minimization, consent-testing, security, and access-record requirements. Taxpayers would fund the new agency.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech, and big platforms

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly and complex: covered entities must run data-minimization analysis, keep records of employee access to sensitive data, and test their consent processes to meet comprehension thresholds the new agency director would set — burdens that scale with company size.

Many duties apply only to larger firms, and the bill gives a nine-month ramp when a company crosses the small-business thresholds, creating a two-tier system; critics reasonably worry that compliance costs fall more easily on large incumbents than on startups and mid-sized competitors.

Consent is not always meaningful: where offering a service without behavioral personalization is infeasible and no core feature can run without it, a company may deny service to someone who refuses to consent.

The bill bans predispute arbitration agreements for claims under the Act, removing a dispute channel many companies rely on, and creating a new federal agency with subpoena and adjudication powers adds a permanent enforcement bureaucracy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy rights are real and broadly useful, and the bill deliberately limits the reach of its core duties to companies that actually profit from data (excluding journalism, security and fraud prevention, and small businesses). The honest costs are compliance burdens concentrated on data-driven firms and the risk that only the biggest companies can comfortably comply — which could entrench the same platforms the bill targets. On balance, for ordinary people the benefits outweigh the costs; the strongest objection is design and cost, not substance.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced and to a subcommittee the next day, no committee ever brought it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo, joined by Rep. Zoe Lofgren, introduced the bill on November 18, 2021.
The same day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary and House Administration Committees.
On November 19, 2021 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the action history for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies whose business depends on collecting and monetizing personal data are better off: no federal privacy rights, no consent requirements, and no new enforcement agency were created, so data-driven business models continued unchanged under the existing patchwork.

sides.party_line_note: All eight named supporters — the sponsor, the co-introducer, and seven cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record of opposition.

industries.note: Their revenue comes from collecting, inferring, and selling personal information. The bill requires consent for disclosure and sale, limits data collection to what is needed for the service, gives users deletion rights, and bans reidentification of 'de-identified' data — directly cutting into that pipeline.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (social media, search, e-commerce)
industries.note: They would lose consent-free targeted advertising and face a new agency plus private lawsuits, but the heaviest compliance obligations — consent-process testing, access records, security systems — fall on firms above the small-business thresholds, which larger incumbents are best positioned to absorb. The bill died, so none of this took effect.
The bill's consent-testing, record-keeping, encryption, and security mandates would create demand for privacy engineering and compliance services. It never passed, so no market opened.
